claims.text: Glacier monitoring is vital for understanding the impacts of climate change and predicting future environmental shifts.
claims.label: why glaciers are monitored

claims.text: Traditional monitoring measured surface elevation changes with surveying equipment such as theodolites and total stations, recording shifts in ice front positions.
claims.label: the traditional survey equipment

claims.text: Modern monitoring relies increasingly on remote sensing: satellite radar and laser altimetry build detailed digital elevation models that reveal changes in ice thickness and surface slope.
claims.label: the satellite remote sensing

claims.text: Ground-based GPS stations supply highly accurate data on ice velocity and deformation.
claims.label: the ground-based GPS stations

claims.text: Ice cores, cylindrical samples drilled from the glacier, are analysed to reconstruct past climate conditions and isotopic ratios.
claims.label: the drilled ice cores

claims.text: Monitoring also assesses meltwater runoff, using gauging stations to measure streamflow and analysing the water's chemical composition.
claims.label: the meltwater runoff measurements

claims.text: Data from these different methods are integrated into glacier inventories and models that inform our understanding of glacial dynamics and global sea-level rise.
claims.label: the integrated glacier models
